prose: An open-source, real-time collaborative Markdown editor (formerly CodiMD). Multiple users edit the same document simultaneously with visible cursors, live preview, and conflict-free merging. Supports slides (reveal.js), diagrams (Mermaid, PlantUML), math (MathJax), tables, and embeds. Great for meeting notes, documentation drafts, and collaborative writing.
entries.pick: you need Google Docs-style real-time collaboration on Markdown documents — meeting notes, design docs, or any content multiple people write together.

alternatives.name: SilverBullet
alternatives.text: HedgeDoc is multi-user real-time collaboration on single documents; SilverBullet is personal knowledge management. HedgeDoc for team writing; SilverBullet for your second brain.

alternatives.name: Joplin Server
alternatives.text: HedgeDoc is collaborative web editing; Joplin is personal encrypted sync. HedgeDoc for shared documents; Joplin for private cross-device notes.

alternatives.name: Memos
alternatives.text: HedgeDoc is for longer collaborative documents; Memos is solo quick-capture. Entirely different use cases.

alternatives.name: Wiki.js
alternatives.text: HedgeDoc excels at real-time co-authoring of individual documents. Wiki.js is a structured wiki with hierarchy, permissions, and search. Use HedgeDoc for live collaboration; Wiki.js for your permanent knowledge base.

categories.label: Photos
categories.description: Photo and video management, backup, and sharing

entries.name: Immich
prose: Google Photos alternative with mobile auto-backup, facial recognition, map view, shared albums, and ML-powered search. Excellent mobile apps (iOS/Android).
> **Note:** Immich is under very active development. Breaking changes between versions are common. Check release notes before upgrading.
entries.pick: you want the closest experience to Google Photos with auto-backup from phone, face detection, and ML search.

alternatives.name: PhotoPrism
alternatives.text: Immich for mobile-first auto-backup workflow; PhotoPrism for existing photo libraries and DAM-style browsing.

entries.name: PhotoPrism
prose: AI-powered photo management that indexes your existing library. Face/object detection, map views, albums. More focused on browsing/organizing than mobile backup.
entries.pick: you have an existing photo library on disk and want to browse it with AI-powered search without moving files around.

alternatives.name: Immich
alternatives.text: PhotoPrism for organizing existing libraries; Immich for phone-to-server auto-backup workflow.

categories.label: Recipes
categories.description: Recipe management, meal planning, and shopping lists

entries.name: Mealie
prose: Self-hosted recipe manager with integrated meal planning, shopping lists, and cookbooks. Import recipes by URL with automatic scraping. REST API for third-party integrations. Vue frontend, Python/FastAPI backend, SQLite or PostgreSQL.
entries.pick: you want the most polished all-in-one experience with meal planning, shopping lists, URL import, multi-user support, and OIDC/LDAP auth — especially if you run a reverse proxy with SSO.

alternatives.name: Tandoor Recipes
alternatives.text: Mealie if you want simpler setup, better mobile UX, and native OIDC; Tandoor if you want more granular permissions, advanced search (trigram), and AI-assisted features.

alternatives.name: RecipeSage
alternatives.text: Mealie if you want a single-container deploy with built-in auth providers; RecipeSage if you want Paprika import compatibility, offline PWA, or collaborative sharing with external users.

entries.name: Tandoor Recipes
prose: Django-based recipe manager built for households. Manage recipes, plan meals, build shopping lists, and organize cookbooks. Powerful search with PostgreSQL trigram similarity. Supports import from many other recipe managers. AI features for image recognition, step sorting, and nutrition lookup.
entries.pick: you want a power-user recipe manager with advanced search, fine-grained permissions for households, AI integrations, and don't mind running PostgreSQL alongside it.

alternatives.name: Mealie
alternatives.text: Tandoor if you need granular space/user permissions, trigram search, or AI-assisted recipe handling; Mealie if you prefer simpler setup and native OIDC.

alternatives.name: RecipeSage
alternatives.text: Tandoor if you want richer household permissions, advanced search, and Django admin flexibility; RecipeSage if you want offline PWA, real-time collaboration, or Paprika-format import.

entries.name: RecipeSage
prose: Collaborative recipe keeper, meal planner, and shopping list organizer delivered as a PWA. Imports from URL, image, PDF, or text. Supports Paprika, Pepperplate, Living Cookbook, Recipe Keeper, CopyMeThat, and CSV import formats. Works offline and syncs across devices. AI cooking assistant, nutrition tracking, recipe scaling with unit conversion.
entries.pick: you're migrating from Paprika or another commercial recipe app and want full import compatibility, offline-first PWA experience, and real-time collaboration on meal plans and shopping lists.

alternatives.name: Mealie
alternatives.text: RecipeSage if you need Paprika/Pepperplate import, offline PWA, or collaborative sharing with family who won't use your SSO; Mealie if you want simpler deploy, OIDC/LDAP auth, and a more traditional server-rendered feel.

alternatives.name: Tandoor Recipes
alternatives.text: RecipeSage if you want offline capability, broader import format support, or a PWA that feels native on mobile; Tandoor if you want Django power-user features, AI image recognition, or household permission spaces.

categories.label: Search
categories.description: Search engines, full-text search, and metasearch aggregators

entries.name: Meilisearch

fields.Auth: API key (master key → generates search/admin keys)

prose: Lightning-fast, typo-tolerant full-text search engine written in Rust. Sub-50ms queries out of the box with zero configuration. RESTful API, faceted search, filtering, sorting, multi-tenancy via tenant tokens, and automatic language detection.
entries.pick: you want instant search with typo tolerance, minimal resource usage, and the simplest possible setup — ideal for app-embedded search (docs sites, e-commerce, internal tools).

alternatives.name: Typesense
alternatives.text: Both are lightweight and developer-friendly. Meilisearch has simpler defaults and broader language support; Typesense has geosearch and more tuning knobs.

alternatives.name: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch
alternatives.text: Meilisearch for instant app search with minimal ops; Elasticsearch for log analytics, complex aggregations, or petabyte scale.

alternatives.name: SearXNG
alternatives.text: Different purpose. Meilisearch indexes your data; SearXNG aggregates external search engines.

entries.name: SearXNG

fields.Auth: none built-in (restrict access via reverse proxy or network)

prose: Privacy-respecting metasearch engine that aggregates results from 70+ search engines (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, etc.) without tracking. Supports web, images, news, videos, science, files, music, and more. Configurable engines, bangs, and result formats.
entries.pick: you want a private, self-hosted search portal that queries multiple engines without leaking your searches to any single provider.

alternatives.name: Meilisearch/Typesense
alternatives.text: Different purpose. SearXNG queries the public internet; Meilisearch/Typesense index your own data.

alternatives.name: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch
alternatives.text: SearXNG is a search frontend/aggregator with zero indexing; Elasticsearch is a search backend that indexes data you feed it.

entries.name: Typesense
prose: Search-as-you-type engine built in C++ with an emphasis on low latency and developer experience. In-memory index for single-digit millisecond responses. Supports faceting, filtering, geosearch, synonyms, curation, and high-availability clustering.
entries.pick: you need sub-5ms search-as-you-type with geosearch, HA clustering, or fine-grained API key scoping — and you're comfortable with slightly more explicit schema configuration.

alternatives.name: Meilisearch
alternatives.text: Typesense has geosearch, joins, vector search, and more explicit schema control. Meilisearch has simpler setup, better typo handling, and broader default language support.

alternatives.name: Elasticsearch/OpenSearch
alternatives.text: Typesense for fast app search with minimal ops; Elasticsearch when you need log aggregation, complex query DSL, or multi-TB indexes.

alternatives.name: SearXNG
alternatives.text: Different purpose. Typesense indexes your data; SearXNG queries external engines.

entries.name: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
prose: Distributed search and analytics engine for structured and unstructured data. Full-text search, log analytics, APM, vector/kNN search, and complex aggregations at scale. OpenSearch is the community-driven Apache-2.0 fork after Elastic's license change. Pairs with Kibana (Elastic) or OpenSearch Dashboards for visualization.

**OpenSearch vs Elasticsearch** — Feature-near-identical. Choose OpenSearch for Apache-2.0 licensing and community governance; Elasticsearch for tighter Kibana integration and faster feature releases from Elastic.
entries.pick: you need distributed full-text search at scale, log/event analytics (ELK/EFK stack), complex aggregations, or a mature ecosystem with extensive plugins and integrations.

alternatives.name: Meilisearch/Typesense
alternatives.text: Elasticsearch for analytics, logs, and complex queries at scale; Meilisearch/Typesense for lightweight instant app search with less operational overhead.

alternatives.name: SearXNG
alternatives.text: Different purpose. Elasticsearch indexes and analyzes your data; SearXNG is a privacy frontend for public search engines.

categories.label: Security & Identity
categories.description: Authentication, identity providers, SSO, password managers, and secrets management

entries.name: Authentik
prose: Full identity provider with flow-based authentication, application proxy, LDAP outpost, and user management. Beautiful admin UI.
entries.pick: you want a modern IdP with visual flow builder, built-in forward-auth proxy, and don't mind the resource usage.

alternatives.name: Keycloak
alternatives.text: Authentik for better UX and built-in proxy; Keycloak for enterprise maturity and broader protocol support.

alternatives.name: Authelia
alternatives.text: Authentik is a full IdP; Authelia is just a forward-auth proxy. Use Authentik if you want SSO for all your apps.

entries.name: Keycloak

fields.Auth: OIDC/OAuth2/SAML provider, LDAP federation, social login

prose: Enterprise-grade IdP by Red Hat. Battle-tested, massive protocol support, but steeper learning curve and heavier footprint.
entries.pick: you need enterprise-grade IdP with full SAML support, user federation, and don't mind Java-level resource usage.

alternatives.name: Authentik
alternatives.text: Keycloak for protocol depth and enterprise track record; Authentik for better DX and integrated proxy.

entries.name: Authelia

fields.Auth: forward-auth proxy (works with Nginx, Traefik, Caddy)

prose: Lightweight authentication and authorization server providing 2FA and SSO via forward-auth headers. Not a full IdP — it sits in front of your reverse proxy.
entries.pick: you just want "add login to any app behind your reverse proxy" without running a full IdP. Extremely lightweight.

alternatives.name: Authentik/Keycloak
alternatives.text: Authelia is not an IdP. It adds auth to apps that don't have it via reverse proxy headers. Use a full IdP if your apps support OIDC natively.

entries.name: Vaultwarden
prose: Lightweight Bitwarden-compatible server written in Rust. Works with all official Bitwarden clients and browser extensions. Unlocks premium features (TOTP, attachments, org vaults) for free.
entries.pick: you want self-hosted password management with Bitwarden's excellent clients but without the official server's heavy .NET stack.

alternatives.name: Bitwarden official
alternatives.text: Vaultwarden for lightweight self-hosting on a homelab; official Bitwarden server if you need enterprise compliance or support contracts.

categories.label: Tasks & Projects
categories.description: Task management, project tracking, kanban boards, and team collaboration

entries.name: Vikunja
prose: A full-featured to-do and project management app with lists, kanban, gantt charts, calendars, and reminders. Single Go binary with a Vue.js frontend — fast, low-resource, and easy to deploy. Supports CalDAV sync, file attachments, labels, priorities, assignees, and recurring tasks.
entries.pick: you want a personal or small-team task manager that covers to-dos, lists, and light project management without the weight of a full PM suite.

alternatives.name: Plane
alternatives.text: Vikunja is lighter and more personal-productivity focused (Todoist/Wunderlist replacement). Plane targets teams doing sprint planning and issue tracking (Jira replacement).

alternatives.name: Huly
alternatives.text: Vikunja is simpler and resource-friendly. Huly bundles docs, chat, and HR alongside task management. Choose Vikunja if you only need tasks.

alternatives.name: Kanboard
alternatives.text: Both are lightweight, but Vikunja has a modern UI, mobile apps, caldav, and more task features. Kanboard is simpler and pure kanban.

entries.name: Plane
prose: Open-source project management tool built as a Jira/Linear alternative. Issues, cycles (sprints), modules, views, pages (docs), and a beautiful UI. Supports custom workflows, bulk operations, analytics dashboards, and intake/triage flows.
entries.pick: you want a modern, team-oriented issue tracker with sprint planning, roadmaps, and a Linear-like UX — and you have the resources to run it.

alternatives.name: Vikunja
alternatives.text: Plane is heavier but purpose-built for team engineering workflows (sprints, modules, roadmaps). Vikunja is better for personal task management.

alternatives.name: Huly
alternatives.text: Both target teams, but Plane focuses on project/issue tracking while Huly bundles chat, docs, and HR. Plane has a more polished issue-tracking UX.

alternatives.name: Kanboard
alternatives.text: Plane is a full PM suite; Kanboard is a minimal kanban board. Plane when you need sprints and analytics; Kanboard when you want simplicity.

entries.name: Huly

fields.Resource: heavy (~1.5GB+; MongoDB + MinIO + Elastic + multiple services)

prose: All-in-one project management platform combining issues, documents, chat, HR, and time tracking. Real-time collaborative editing, Slack-like communication, and a polished UI. Aims to replace Linear + Notion + Slack in one self-hosted package.
entries.pick: you want a single platform for project management, team chat, and documentation — and you have the resources to run a larger stack.

alternatives.name: Vikunja
alternatives.text: Huly is far heavier and team-focused. Vikunja is ideal for personal to-dos and light project work without the overhead.

alternatives.name: Plane
alternatives.text: Huly bundles more (chat, docs, HR); Plane has a more focused and polished issue-tracking experience. Choose Plane for engineering PM, Huly if you want fewer separate tools.

alternatives.name: Kanboard
alternatives.text: Completely different weight classes. Kanboard for minimal kanban; Huly for teams wanting an integrated workspace.

entries.name: Kanboard

fields.Auth: built-in, LDAP, OIDC (via plugin), reverse proxy auth

prose: Minimalist kanban board focused on simplicity. No bloat — drag-and-drop tasks across columns, swimlanes, subtasks, time tracking, and analytics. Plugin system for extending functionality. Works great on low-powered hardware.
entries.pick: you want a dead-simple, no-frills kanban board with the smallest footprint and easy maintenance.

alternatives.name: Vikunja
alternatives.text: Kanboard is purer kanban with a more spartan UI. Vikunja has a modern interface, multiple views (list/kanban/gantt/calendar), and mobile apps.

alternatives.name: Plane
alternatives.text: Kanboard is minimal and personal; Plane is a full team PM suite. Kanboard if you just need cards on a board; Plane for sprint planning and roadmaps.

alternatives.name: Huly
alternatives.text: Kanboard for solo lightweight kanban; Huly for teams wanting an integrated all-in-one platform.

categories.label: Video Surveillance
categories.description: NVR, camera management, motion detection, and AI-powered monitoring

entries.name: Frigate

fields.Resource: heavy (~1GB idle; AI accelerator strongly recommended — Coral TPU or GPU)

prose: AI-powered NVR with realtime local object detection for IP cameras. Uses TensorFlow/OpenVINO/ONNX for detection, supports Google Coral TPU and various GPU accelerators. Tight Home Assistant integration via MQTT and a custom component. Features include 24/7 recording, motion-triggered object detection, zone-based alerts, RTSP re-streaming, WebRTC live view, and a review workflow for events.
entries.pick: you want the best-in-class AI object detection NVR, use Home Assistant, or have a Coral TPU / GPU available for inference. The modern UI, active community, and detection accuracy make it the top choice for homelabbers.

alternatives.name: ZoneMinder
alternatives.text: Frigate if you want modern AI detection, better UX, and Home Assistant integration; ZoneMinder if you need a traditional CCTV platform with decades of maturity, PTZ control, or zone-based legacy motion detection.

alternatives.name: Viseron
alternatives.text: Frigate if you want the larger community, better docs, polished UI, and Home Assistant support; Viseron if you want face recognition built-in or prefer a more modular/plugin architecture.

alternatives.name: Shinobi
alternatives.text: Frigate if you want AI detection and modern architecture; Shinobi if you need multi-tenant accounts, browser-based management for many cameras, or don't need AI.

entries.name: ZoneMinder
prose: Traditional open-source CCTV software with 20+ years of development. Supports IP, USB, and analog cameras. Features include zone-based motion detection, PTZ control, event recording, email/SMS alerts, multi-user access control, and an API. Can be extended with machine learning via the Event Notification Server (zmeventnotification) for object/face detection.
entries.pick: you want a battle-tested, feature-complete CCTV platform with granular zone configuration, PTZ support, and don't mind the legacy UI. Good for large camera counts with traditional motion detection requirements.

alternatives.name: Frigate
alternatives.text: ZoneMinder if you want PTZ control, traditional zone-based motion detection, or need the maturity of a 20-year-old project; Frigate if you want modern AI detection, better UX, and lower-latency live views.

alternatives.name: Viseron
alternatives.text: ZoneMinder if you need traditional CCTV features (PTZ, multi-user); Viseron if you want a more modern AI-first approach without the legacy baggage.

alternatives.name: Shinobi
alternatives.text: ZoneMinder if you want GPL licensing and proven stability; Shinobi if you prefer a modern Node.js stack and multi-tenant architecture.

entries.name: Viseron

fields.Resource: heavy (~1GB; GPU recommended for AI — supports CUDA, VAAPI, EdgeTPU, Hailo)

prose: Self-hosted, local-only NVR with AI computer vision. Features object detection, motion detection, face recognition, license plate recognition, and post-processing. Modular component architecture supports multiple detection backends (DeepStack, CodeProject.AI, YOLO, EdgeTPU, Hailo). Includes a web UI with live views and event browsing.
entries.pick: you want built-in face recognition or license plate detection, prefer a modular plugin architecture, or want to run multiple AI backends simultaneously. Good alternative to Frigate if you don't use Home Assistant.

alternatives.name: Frigate
alternatives.text: Viseron if you want native face recognition, don't use Home Assistant, or prefer its plugin system; Frigate if you want larger community, better docs, more polished UI, and tighter HA integration.

alternatives.name: ZoneMinder
alternatives.text: Viseron if you want modern AI without legacy baggage; ZoneMinder if you need PTZ, multi-user, or traditional CCTV features.

alternatives.name: Shinobi
alternatives.text: Viseron if you want AI-first with face/plate recognition; Shinobi if you need multi-tenant management or a simpler non-AI setup.

entries.name: Shinobi
prose: Open-source CCTV platform written in Node.js. Designed for multi-account/multi-tenant use with WebSocket-based streaming. Supports 6000+ camera models via ONVIF/RTSP/MJPEG. Features include motion detection, recording schedules, two-factor auth, plugin system for object detection (via external plugins), and a developer-friendly API.
entries.pick: you need multi-tenant camera management (separate accounts per user/site), want a modern Node.js stack, or need an API-first platform for integration. Good for small businesses managing cameras across multiple locations.

alternatives.name: Frigate
alternatives.text: Shinobi if you need multi-tenant accounts or don't need AI; Frigate if you want object detection, Home Assistant integration, and active development.

alternatives.name: ZoneMinder
alternatives.text: Shinobi if you want modern architecture, multi-tenant, and WebSocket streaming; ZoneMinder if you want GPL licensing, PTZ control, and proven long-term stability.

alternatives.name: Viseron
alternatives.text: Shinobi if you need multi-user accounts and simpler non-AI recording; Viseron if you want native AI detection and face recognition.

categories.label: VPN & Remote Access
categories.description: VPN servers, mesh networking, remote desktop, and tunneling

entries.name: WireGuard

fields.Resource: minimal (~10MB kernel module; ~50MB with GUI wrapper)

prose: Extremely fast, modern VPN protocol built into the Linux kernel. Minimal attack surface (~4000 lines of code), cryptographically sound (Noise protocol framework), and outperforms IPsec/OpenVPN on throughput and latency.
entries.pick: you want raw VPN performance with minimal overhead, already manage your own key distribution, or need a single point-to-point or hub-and-spoke tunnel without extra dependencies.

alternatives.name: Tailscale/Headscale
alternatives.text: WireGuard for raw protocol control and zero dependencies; Tailscale/Headscale for automatic key exchange, NAT traversal, and mesh topology.

alternatives.name: NetBird
alternatives.text: WireGuard for simplicity and kernel-level speed; NetBird for managed mesh with SSO and ACLs on top of WireGuard.

alternatives.name: OpenVPN
alternatives.text: WireGuard for speed, simplicity, and modern crypto; OpenVPN for legacy compatibility and TCP fallback.

entries.name: Tailscale / Headscale

fields.Auth: SSO via identity provider (Tailscale SaaS); OIDC (Headscale)

prose: Mesh VPN built on WireGuard that handles key exchange, NAT traversal (DERP relays), and peer discovery automatically. Tailscale is the hosted SaaS; Headscale is the self-hosted, open-source control server implementing the Tailscale coordination protocol.
entries.pick: you want zero-config mesh networking across NATs with automatic peer discovery, MagicDNS, and ACLs — especially if you want to self-host the control plane (Headscale).

alternatives.name: WireGuard
alternatives.text: Tailscale/Headscale for automatic mesh topology, NAT traversal, and SSO; raw WireGuard for maximum control and no coordination server.

alternatives.name: NetBird
alternatives.text: Tailscale/Headscale for maturity and ecosystem (Funnel, Serve, exit nodes); NetBird for native OIDC integration, network policies, and self-hosted-first design.

alternatives.name: Nebula
alternatives.text: Tailscale/Headscale for ease of setup and richer features; Nebula for certificate-based auth and Slack-backed pedigree.

entries.name: NetBird

fields.Auth: OIDC / SSO (Authentik, Keycloak, Zitadel, Auth0, Google, etc.)

prose: Mesh networking platform that combines WireGuard tunnels with SSO-based identity, network policies (ACLs, routes, DNS), and NAT traversal. Self-hosted-first architecture with a management UI for peer groups, access control, and posture checks.
entries.pick: you want a self-hosted mesh VPN with first-class SSO integration (e.g., Authentik), granular network policies, and a management UI — especially in a homelab already running an IdP.

alternatives.name: Tailscale/Headscale
alternatives.text: NetBird for native self-hosted design with rich ACLs and SSO from day one; Tailscale/Headscale for maturity, larger community, and extra features (Funnel, exit nodes).

alternatives.name: WireGuard
alternatives.text: NetBird for managed mesh with identity-based access; WireGuard for raw tunnel performance with manual key management.

alternatives.name: ZeroTier
alternatives.text: NetBird for WireGuard-based speed and OIDC auth; ZeroTier for layer-2 virtual networking and longer track record.

entries.name: Guacamole

fields.Resource: medium (~500MB; Java client + C daemon + DB)
fields.Auth: built-in (database) + OIDC, LDAP, SAML, TOTP, header auth

prose: Clientless remote desktop gateway — access RDP, VNC, SSH, Telnet, and Kubernetes terminals through a web browser with no plugins or client software required. Supports session recording, file transfer, and multi-factor auth.
entries.pick: you want browser-based remote access to desktops and servers without installing client software — ideal for accessing Windows machines, jumpboxes, or lab hosts from any device.

alternatives.name: RustDesk
alternatives.text: Guacamole for browser-based access to existing RDP/VNC/SSH; RustDesk for peer-to-peer remote desktop with its own client.

alternatives.name: MeshCentral
alternatives.text: Guacamole for protocol-gateway simplicity (RDP/VNC/SSH via browser); MeshCentral for full remote management suite with agents, file transfer, and device inventory.

alternatives.name: Apache NiFi + SSH
alternatives.text: Guacamole for interactive GUI/terminal sessions; direct SSH/RDP for scripted access without a web layer.

entries.name: Neon
prose: Serverless Postgres that scales to zero.
entries.pick: you need real Postgres with zero cold-start cost, instant branching for preview deployments, and you refuse to babysit connection pools or idle instances.

alternatives.name: Supabase
alternatives.text: Neon is pure database; pick Supabase when you also want auth, storage, and REST auto-generated from your schema. Pick Neon when you want raw Postgres control without BaaS opinions.

alternatives.name: Turso
alternatives.text: Neon gives you full Postgres (joins, extensions, JSONB); Turso gives you SQLite semantics with edge-local reads. Pick Turso for read-heavy global apps; pick Neon for complex relational queries and migrations tooling.

entries.name: Turso
prose: LibSQL at the edge — strong for read-heavy apps.
entries.pick: your app is read-heavy (dashboards, content sites, analytics) and you want embedded replicas that sit next to your compute for sub-millisecond reads without a connection round-trip.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare D1
alternatives.text: Both are SQLite-at-edge. Pick D1 if you're already on Cloudflare Workers and want zero-config binding. Pick Turso if you deploy on Vercel/Fly/Deno and need a portable edge DB with embedded replicas you control.

alternatives.name: Neon
alternatives.text: Pick Turso when reads dominate and you want edge locality. Pick Neon when you need Postgres features (CTEs, full-text search, extensions) or write-heavy transactional workloads.

entries.name: Supabase

fields.Limits: 0.5 GB DB · 50k MAU · pauses after 7d idle

prose: Postgres BaaS with auth, storage, and REST out of the box.
entries.pick: you want a complete backend — auth, file storage, realtime subscriptions, and auto-generated REST/GraphQL — without stitching separate services together, and you still want raw Postgres access when the abstractions aren't enough.

alternatives.name: Appwrite Cloud
alternatives.text: Both are BaaS. Pick Supabase when you want real Postgres underneath (migrations, extensions, SQL). Pick Appwrite when you prefer a self-hostable, vendor-neutral platform with a simpler permissions model.

alternatives.name: Neon
alternatives.text: Pick Supabase when you want the full platform (auth, storage, edge functions) in one dashboard. Pick Neon when you only need the database and want to pair it with your own auth/storage choices.

entries.name: Upstash Redis
prose: Serverless Redis for cache and queues.
entries.pick: you need a fast key-value layer for caching, rate-limiting, session tokens, or lightweight queues — and you want per-request pricing with no always-on instance to manage.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare KV/D1
alternatives.text: Pick Upstash when you need Redis data structures (sorted sets, pub/sub, Lua scripts) or when your stack isn't on Cloudflare. Pick D1/KV when you're already on Workers and want zero-network-hop access.

alternatives.name: a primary database (Neon/Turso)
alternatives.text: Upstash is a complement, not a replacement. Use it as the caching/queue layer in front of your relational store, not as your source of truth.

entries.name: Convex
prose: Reactive backend with realtime sync for collaborative UIs.
entries.pick: you're building a collaborative or realtime-first app (multiplayer editors, live dashboards, chat) in TypeScript and you want the database, server functions, and realtime subscriptions as one coherent system — no SQL, no ORM, no WebSocket plumbing.

alternatives.name: Supabase Realtime
alternatives.text: Supabase bolts realtime onto Postgres via change-data-capture; Convex is reactive from the ground up. Pick Convex when every query must live-update. Pick Supabase when you also need traditional REST endpoints and raw SQL escape hatches.

alternatives.name: Firebase
alternatives.text: Convex gives you TypeScript-native server functions with full ACID transactions; Firebase gives you a proprietary SDK with weaker consistency. Pick Convex for type-safe, transactional realtime; Firebase if you need its massive mobile ecosystem.

entries.name: Cloudflare D1

fields.Limits: 5 GB / DB · 5M rows read/day on free Workers

prose: SQLite at the edge on Workers.
entries.pick: you're already on Cloudflare Workers and want a database that's a first-class binding — zero network hop, zero connection overhead, deployed alongside your code at the edge.

alternatives.name: Turso
alternatives.text: Both are edge SQLite. Pick D1 when your compute is Workers (native binding, no SDK needed). Pick Turso when you deploy elsewhere (Vercel, Fly, Deno) or need embedded replicas inside your app process.

alternatives.name: Neon
alternatives.text: Pick D1 for simple schemas and edge-speed reads on Workers. Pick Neon when you need full Postgres (complex joins, extensions, large write throughput) or when your app lives outside the Cloudflare ecosystem.

entries.name: MongoDB Atlas M0
prose: Classic document store, free forever shared cluster.
entries.pick: your data is naturally document-shaped (nested objects, variable fields per record), you want a flexible schema that evolves without migrations, and you value the massive MongoDB ecosystem (Mongoose, Atlas Search, Charts).

alternatives.name: Neon/Supabase
alternatives.text: Pick MongoDB when your data doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns (CMS entries, event logs, IoT payloads). Pick Postgres (Neon/Supabase) when you need relational integrity, joins, and strong typing.

alternatives.name: Convex
alternatives.text: Both handle schema-flexible data. Pick Convex for realtime-first TypeScript apps. Pick MongoDB when you want a mature query language (aggregation pipeline), driver support in every language, and a proven path to massive scale.

entries.name: Appwrite Cloud
prose: Auth + DB + Functions in one BaaS.
entries.pick: you want a Firebase-like all-in-one platform (auth, database, functions, storage) that's fully open-source and self-hostable — giving you an exit door that proprietary BaaS platforms don't offer.

alternatives.name: Supabase
alternatives.text: Both are open-source BaaS. Pick Supabase when you want real Postgres and SQL power. Pick Appwrite when you prefer a document-style API, simpler permission rules, and don't need raw SQL.

alternatives.name: PocketBase
alternatives.text: Both are self-hostable. Pick PocketBase for a single-binary zero-dependency deploy on one VPS. Pick Appwrite when you need managed cloud hosting, multiple runtimes for functions, and a larger team/community behind the platform.

entries.name: PocketBase
prose: Single-binary BaaS — SQLite, auth, files, realtime without a cloud bill.
entries.pick: you want the simplest possible self-hosted backend — one binary, no Docker required, zero monthly cost on a free-tier VPS — and your app is small-to-medium scale where SQLite's single-writer model is fine.

alternatives.name: Supabase
alternatives.text: Pick PocketBase when you want total ownership with no cloud dependency and your traffic fits one machine. Pick Supabase when you need horizontal scale, managed infra, and Postgres features.

alternatives.name: Appwrite
alternatives.text: Both are open-source BaaS. Pick PocketBase for radical simplicity (single Go binary, embed in your app). Pick Appwrite for a richer feature set (multiple function runtimes, team collaboration, managed cloud option).

entries.pick: your app is a static frontend + API routes and you want zero cold starts at the edge with the most generous free static tier available — no bandwidth caps, no sleep, no containers to manage.

alternatives.name: Vercel Hobby:
alternatives.text: Both deploy static + functions, but Workers runs on 300+ edge locations with no commercial-use restriction; Vercel locks you to hobby/non-commercial on the free plan. **vs Render:** Render gives you a container that sleeps after 15 min; Workers never sleeps and responds in <50 ms globally.

entries.name: Koyeb
prose: Managed containers that stay up 24/7 on free micro.
entries.pick: you need a container that never sleeps — Discord bots, background workers, or long-running processes that must stay warm without paying. Koyeb's free micro runs 24/7 with zero cold-start penalty.

alternatives.name: Render:
alternatives.text: Render's free web services sleep after 15 min of inactivity (30–60 s cold starts); Koyeb stays awake permanently. **vs Railway:** Railway gives ~$5/mo in credits that run out; Koyeb's free instance is truly unlimited hours.

entries.name: Vercel Hobby
prose: Next.js-native deploys. Personal projects only.
entries.pick: you're building a Next.js side project and want the tightest integration possible — ISR, middleware, image optimization, and preview deployments all work out of the box with zero config. Accept the non-commercial restriction and enjoy the DX.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Pages:
alternatives.text: Cloudflare allows commercial use and has no bandwidth cap, but Next.js support is partial (no streaming RSC, limited middleware); Vercel is the canonical Next.js host. **vs Netlify:** Netlify also deploys Next.js but lags behind on latest features and has tighter build-minute limits.

entries.name: Railway
prose: Git-push containers with a small monthly credit.
entries.pick: you want the simplest git-push-to-deploy container experience with databases, cron, and private networking included — and you're okay spending $5/mo once the free credit runs out. Railway treats containers as first-class: Postgres, Redis, and workers all live in one project.

alternatives.name: Render:
alternatives.text: Render's free tier sleeps and the free Postgres expires after 30 days; Railway's $5 credit covers always-on compute + persistent DB. **vs Koyeb:** Koyeb gives you one always-free micro, but Railway gives a full project graph (app + DB + worker) under one credit pool.

entries.name: Render

fields.Limits: 750 hrs/mo · sleep after 15m · free Postgres expires 30d

prose: Web services without a credit card. Sleeps when idle.
entries.pick: you want to ship a demo or portfolio app with zero financial commitment — no credit card, no trial expiry, no surprise bills. The 15-minute sleep is fine for anything that tolerates a cold start on first hit (portfolio sites, demo APIs, interview take-homes).

alternatives.name: Koyeb:
alternatives.text: Koyeb never sleeps but limits you to one 512 MB micro; Render gives 750 free hours across multiple services (useful for multi-service demos). **vs Railway:** Railway requires a credit card and charges after credits are gone; Render stays free forever if you accept the sleep trade-off.

matrixCells.limits: 750 hrs/mo · sleep after 15m · free Postgres expires 30d

entries.name: Netlify
prose: JAMstack hosting + serverless functions.
entries.pick: you're shipping a static site or SPA that needs a few serverless functions for forms, auth, or API proxying — and you want 100 GB bandwidth free without worrying about cold containers or edge-runtime constraints. Netlify's build plugins and form handling are unmatched for content sites.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Pages:
alternatives.text: Cloudflare has no bandwidth cap and faster edge functions, but Netlify's build plugin ecosystem (CMS previews, form handling, split testing) is richer for content-heavy JAMstack. **vs Vercel Hobby:** Netlify allows commercial use on the free tier; Vercel Hobby restricts you to non-commercial projects.

entries.name: Deno Deploy
prose: TypeScript at the edge; pairs with Deno KV.
entries.pick: you're writing TypeScript/Deno-native code and want an edge runtime with built-in KV storage — no external database required for small apps. 1M requests/month free makes it viable for real production traffic, not just demos.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Workers:
alternatives.text: Both are edge runtimes, but Deno Deploy uses standard Web APIs + Deno KV with zero config; Workers requires learning KV/D1 bindings and the Cloudflare-specific module system. **vs Vercel Edge Functions:** Vercel's edge runtime is a thin layer on top of their Node platform; Deno Deploy is the runtime itself with first-party KV, giving you a complete backend in one place.

entries.name: Oracle Cloud Always Free

fields.Limits: 2× AMD VMs + 4 ARM OCPUs · 200 GB block

prose: Real VMs forever — if you survive signup.
entries.pick: you need actual Linux VMs with root access, persistent storage, and serious compute (4 ARM OCPUs + 24 GB RAM is more than most $50/mo VPS plans) — and you're patient enough to fight Oracle's signup lottery. Once provisioned, these run any stack: Docker, K3s, databases, game servers, whatever.

alternatives.name: Koyeb/Render/Railway:
alternatives.text: Those are managed PaaS with opinionated runtimes; Oracle gives you bare metal control — install anything, run anything, no platform lock-in. **vs Fly.io:** Fly gives you global distribution but charges per GB/hour; Oracle gives you one region but 24 GB RAM free forever.

matrixCells.limits: 2× AMD VMs + 4 ARM OCPUs · 200 GB block

entries.name: Coolify

fields.Limits: OSS · unlimited apps on your infra

prose: Self-hosted PaaS — Heroku/Render shape on your VPS.
entries.pick: you already have a VPS (Oracle Always Free, Hetzner, etc.) and want a Heroku-like UI for deploying unlimited apps without per-service fees. Coolify handles git deploys, SSL, databases, and backups — you own the entire stack.

alternatives.name: Railway/Render:
alternatives.text: Those charge per service or impose free-tier limits; Coolify is free and unlimited — you only pay for the underlying VM. **vs Oracle Cloud alone:** Oracle gives you the VM but no deployment tooling; Coolify turns that raw VM into a one-click PaaS with auto-SSL and Docker Compose support.

entries.name: Clerk
prose: Pre-built auth UI for B2B/B2C.
entries.pick: you want auth working in an afternoon, not a weekend — drop-in `<SignIn/>` components, hosted account portal, and you never write a password-reset flow again. 50 k monthly active users before you pay a cent means most indie projects never outgrow free.

alternatives.name: Kinde:
alternatives.text: Clerk's UI components are richer out-of-the-box (pre-styled modals, user profile pages); Kinde bundles feature flags and SSO at the same tier so you install fewer vendors. Pick Clerk for speed-to-ship; pick Kinde if you also need flags/SSO without another tool.

alternatives.name: Zitadel:
alternatives.text: Clerk is a managed-only service — zero ops, but you can't self-host. Zitadel gives you an OSS escape hatch and 25 k MAU free, but you build your own login UI.

entries.name: Kinde
prose: Auth with SSO and feature flags.
entries.pick: you need auth, enterprise SSO, and feature flags from one vendor so you're not duct-taping Clerk + LaunchDarkly together. Kinde's free tier (~10.5 k MAU) is lower than Clerk's, but the bundled flags and RBAC make it the better consolidated choice for B2B SaaS that will need "is this feature enabled for org X?" logic from day one.

alternatives.name: Clerk:
alternatives.text: Kinde trades Clerk's polished UI kit for built-in feature flags, roles, and SSO — fewer vendors, but you'll style your own login screens. Pick Kinde when your app needs gating and org-level access control early; pick Clerk when pixel-perfect auth UX matters more than bundled infra.

entries.name: Doppler

fields.Limits: 5 users free · Team free via GitHub Pack while student

prose: Secrets sync to Vercel, Koyeb, Railway.
entries.pick: your stack spans multiple deploy targets (Vercel preview + Railway prod + local dev) and you're tired of copy-pasting `.env` values between dashboards. Doppler becomes the single source of truth for secrets and syncs them to each target automatically — one `doppler run` replaces a pile of `.env` files.

alternatives.name: Infisical:
alternatives.text: Doppler is polished SaaS with first-class integrations for Vercel/Railway/Fly; Infisical is open-source and self-hostable. Pick Doppler for zero-ops secret sync across commercial PaaS; pick Infisical if you want an auditable OSS layer you control or need to avoid vendor lock-in on secrets.

matrixCells.limits: 5 users free · Team free via GitHub Pack while student

entries.name: Hookdeck
prose: Webhook ingest with retries and queues.
entries.pick: you receive webhooks from Stripe/Clerk/GitHub and need guaranteed delivery without writing your own retry queue. Hookdeck sits in front of your endpoint, buffers events, retries failures with backoff, and gives you a replay UI — 100 k events/mo free is plenty for indie SaaS webhook traffic.

alternatives.name: rolling your own:
alternatives.text: A custom Bull/Redis queue gives you full control but costs a VPS and maintenance. Hookdeck is zero-infra: point the provider's webhook URL at Hookdeck, point Hookdeck at your app, and get retries + observability for free. Pick Hookdeck until your event volume or latency needs outgrow the managed tier.

entries.name: Infisical

fields.Limits: Free cloud tier for secrets sync

prose: Open-source Doppler alternative.
entries.pick: you want secret management you can audit, fork, and self-host — no vendor can pull the rug on your secrets infra. Infisical's cloud free tier works like Doppler (env sync, integrations), but you also get the option to run it on your own box for compliance or air-gapped setups.

alternatives.name: Doppler:
alternatives.text: Infisical is OSS-first — you can self-host, audit the code, and avoid proprietary lock-in. Doppler has slicker PaaS integrations (one-click Vercel sync) and a more polished CLI UX. Pick Infisical when sovereignty and self-host matter; pick Doppler when you just want secrets to flow to managed platforms with zero ops.

matrixCells.limits: Free cloud tier for secrets sync

entries.name: Zitadel

fields.Limits: ~25k MAU free cloud · OSS self-host unlimited

prose: Cloud-native IdP with passkeys and multi-tenancy — Clerk alternative.
entries.pick: you want a full identity provider (OIDC/SAML/passkeys) you can self-host long-term without per-MAU pricing cliffs. Zitadel's free cloud gives you 25 k MAU to validate, and the OSS binary means you can move to your own infra when margins matter — no rewrite, same API.

alternatives.name: Clerk:
alternatives.text: Zitadel is an IdP you own; Clerk is a widget you rent. Clerk ships faster (drag-and-drop UI), but Zitadel gives you protocol-level control (custom OIDC scopes, SAML federation, machine-to-machine tokens) and no hard vendor ceiling. Pick Zitadel for multi-tenant B2B that will eventually need self-hosted auth; pick Clerk if you want login done in a day and won't self-host.

matrixCells.limits: ~25k MAU free cloud · OSS self-host unlimited

entries.name: Resend
prose: Transactional email with React Email DX.
entries.pick: your app sends password resets, receipts, or magic links and you want to compose them in JSX/TSX like a React component — not raw HTML tables from 2004. The 3k/mo free tier covers early-stage SaaS without thinking about cost, and the single-domain cap only hurts if you run multiple brands.

alternatives.name: Brevo
alternatives.text: Resend is pure transactional with a modern SDK; Brevo bundles marketing lists and campaigns you won't use yet. **vs SendGrid** — Resend's deliverability is comparable but the DX (React Email templates, instant logs) is a generation ahead of SendGrid's legacy dashboard.

entries.name: Brevo
prose: Marketing + transactional in one forever-free tier.
entries.pick: you need both drip campaigns (welcome sequences, newsletters) and transactional sends (order confirmations) from one platform without stitching two services together. The 300 emails/day forever-free tier is generous enough for a side-project that also wants to nurture a small subscriber list.

alternatives.name: Resend
alternatives.text: Brevo adds a full marketing automation UI; Resend is code-only transactional. **vs Loops** — Brevo is broader (CRM, SMS, chat) but less opinionated about SaaS lifecycle; Loops is purpose-built for product-led onboarding flows.

entries.name: Loops
prose: Product/lifecycle email for SaaS onboarding.
entries.pick: you're building a SaaS and your emails are event-driven: "user signed up → send welcome", "trial day 3 → nudge to activate", "plan cancelled → win-back". Loops is designed around product events, not marketing blasts — the 1k contacts free tier fits pre-PMF perfectly.

alternatives.name: Brevo
alternatives.text: Loops speaks product events natively (user.signed_up, subscription.cancelled); Brevo forces you to map those into generic automation triggers. **vs Resend** — Resend is a pipe (send this template now); Loops owns the timing, segmentation, and sequence logic so you don't build it yourself.

entries.name: Tally / Formspark
prose: Drop-in forms without standing up a backend.
entries.pick: you need a contact form, waitlist signup, or feedback widget on a static site or landing page and refuse to spin up an API just to receive a POST. Tally gives you a Notion-like form builder with unlimited submissions on free; Formspark is a minimal `<form action>` endpoint if you want full HTML control.

alternatives.name: Formspree
alternatives.text: Tally's free tier is far more generous (unlimited submissions vs 50/mo) and the builder is nicer; Formspree wins only if you need its plugin ecosystem or paid validations. **vs building your own** — a serverless function + DB costs $0 too, but takes an afternoon you could spend on your actual product.

entries.name: Twilio Trial

fields.Limits: Trial credit · numbers can be restricted · PAYG after

prose: SMS/voice for OTP and alerts — trial credit, then meter hard.
entries.pick: you need phone-number verification or SMS OTP codes and want the widest global carrier coverage with battle-tested docs. Twilio's trial credit lets you prototype the full flow for free; just know that after the credit burns you're paying per-message with no free floor.

alternatives.name: Vonage
alternatives.text: Twilio has superior documentation, broader SDK support, and more phone-number inventory in most countries. Choose Vonage only when Twilio can't provision a number in your target region or its per-message rate is notably worse there. **vs email OTP** — SMS adds real friction and cost; only use it when regulatory or UX requirements demand phone verification.

matrixCells.limits: Trial credit · numbers can be restricted · PAYG after

entries.name: Vonage (Nexmo)
prose: SMS/voice alternative when Twilio pricing or coverage is awkward.
entries.pick: Twilio can't provision a local number in your target country, charges an unreasonable premium on a specific route, or you want a second vendor for failover. Vonage's API surface is comparable but the signup credit is stingy — treat it as a backup, not a default.

alternatives.name: Twilio
alternatives.text: Vonage occasionally wins on per-SMS pricing in APAC/EMEA corridors and has better WhatsApp Business API coverage in some regions; Twilio wins everywhere else on DX, docs, and ecosystem. **vs email-based OTP** — same trade-off as Twilio: only reach for SMS when a phone number is the trust anchor your product needs.

entries.name: Postmark
prose: Transactional email with serious deliverability — trial then paid.
entries.pick: inbox placement is non-negotiable — invoices, security alerts, or anything where "check your spam folder" is unacceptable. Postmark's entire business model is deliverability-first (they reject bulk marketing senders). The catch: there's no forever-free tier, so use it once your product earns revenue or when you graduate from Resend/SendGrid's free caps.

alternatives.name: Resend
alternatives.text: Postmark has years of deliverability reputation data and dedicated IPs at lower volumes; Resend is newer but the free tier and DX are better for pre-revenue. **vs SendGrid** — Postmark's sending reputation is pristine because they refuse marketing mail; SendGrid's shared IPs are diluted by everyone else's newsletters.

entries.name: Twilio SendGrid

fields.Limits: Free forever ~100 emails/day class · verify current Free plan

prose: Legacy free forever email tier — still useful, watch reputation limits.
entries.pick: you want a permanent free floor (~100 emails/day) for transactional sends and don't mind an older dashboard. SendGrid's free plan has survived multiple Twilio policy changes — verify it still exists before onboarding — but it works if you just need password resets and don't want to think about billing.

alternatives.name: Resend
alternatives.text: SendGrid has more email volume on free (100/day vs Resend's 100/day but 3k/mo cap), but Resend's developer experience, logging, and template tooling are dramatically better. **vs Postmark** — SendGrid is free; Postmark is paid. If you don't yet have revenue and can tolerate shared-IP reputation risk, SendGrid costs nothing.

matrixCells.limits: Free forever ~100 emails/day class · verify current Free plan

entries.name: Formspree
prose: Form backend for static sites — email on submit without a server.
entries.pick: you want a zero-JS form endpoint you can drop into any HTML page with a simple `action=` URL — no build step, no SDK, no client-side code required. The 50 submissions/mo free cap is tight, so this fits low-traffic pages like a portfolio contact form or an internal feedback widget.

alternatives.name: Tally
alternatives.text: Formspree is a raw HTTP endpoint (you own the HTML); Tally is a hosted form builder (you embed their UI). Pick Formspree when you want pixel-perfect form styling. **vs Formspark** — nearly identical concept; Formspree has a slightly richer plugin/integration layer, Formspark is simpler and cheaper at paid tiers.

entries.name: Forward Email

fields.Limits: Unlimited aliases free class · paid for outbound SMTP

prose: Privacy-first custom-domain email forwarding — free MX without a mailbox bill.
entries.pick: you want `hello@yourdomain.com` to land in your personal Gmail/Proton without paying for Google Workspace or a hosted mailbox. Forward Email gives unlimited aliases on the free tier — perfect for receiving support@ or billing@ at your custom domain while keeping a single inbox.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare Email Routing
alternatives.text: both are free inbound forwarding; Forward Email is open-source and works with any DNS provider, while Cloudflare Email Routing requires your domain's nameservers on Cloudflare. **vs ImprovMX** — Forward Email's free tier is more generous (unlimited aliases vs 25) and the project is fully open-source with no tracking.

entries.name: Cloudflare R2

fields.Limits: 10 GB · 1M Class A · 10M Class B · $0 egress

prose: S3-compatible object storage with zero egress fees.
entries.pick: you need general-purpose object storage and refuse to pay egress taxes — especially if you're already on Cloudflare Workers or Pages. The 10 GB free tier plus zero egress makes it the default choice for any project that serves files to users.

alternatives.name: Backblaze B2:
alternatives.text: R2 gives you zero egress natively; B2 only waives egress if you route through Cloudflare CDN. R2 also has tighter Workers integration (bindings, no auth overhead). Pick B2 only for cold archive you rarely read.

alternatives.name: Tigris:
alternatives.text: Both are S3-compatible, but R2 is battle-tested at Cloudflare scale with richer ecosystem tooling. Tigris wins if your compute lives on Fly and you want automatic edge replication without CDN config.

matrixCells.limits: 10 GB · 1M Class A · 10M Class B · $0 egress

entries.name: Backblaze B2
prose: Cheap archive storage; egress waived via Cloudflare.
entries.pick: you have cold data (backups, exports, user archives) that's written once and rarely read — and you want the absolute cheapest $/GB at rest. Pair it with a Cloudflare CDN zone to get free egress via the Bandwidth Alliance.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare R2:
alternatives.text: B2 is cheaper per GB stored ($0.005 vs $0.015), but R2's zero egress is unconditional and doesn't require CDN fronting. If you read files frequently, R2 wins on total cost. B2 is the budget cold-storage play.

alternatives.name: Tigris:
alternatives.text: B2 has no edge replication or smart caching — it's a single-region bucket. Tigris is better if latency matters; B2 is better if you just want a cheap vault.

entries.name: UploadThing
prose: File uploads wired for Next.js in minutes.
entries.pick: you're building a Next.js app and want file uploads working in under 30 minutes with zero infra config — presigned URLs, progress callbacks, type-safe routes, and a dashboard included. The 2 GB free tier is tight but perfect for MVPs and prototypes.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare R2:
alternatives.text: R2 gives you raw S3 buckets — you'll wire presigned URLs and client uploaders yourself. UploadThing is a managed upload layer with built-in UI components and callbacks. Pick R2 when you outgrow 2 GB or need full control; pick UploadThing when speed-to-ship matters more.

alternatives.name: Cloudinary:
alternatives.text: Cloudinary transforms media after upload; UploadThing just stores and serves files. If you need resizing, cropping, or format conversion, Cloudinary is the tool. If you just need "user uploads a file, app stores it," UploadThing is simpler.

entries.name: Cloudinary
prose: On-the-fly image and video transforms.
entries.pick: your app is image-heavy or video-heavy and you need resize, crop, format conversion, watermarking, or adaptive streaming without running your own pipeline. The URL-based transform API means zero server code for media manipulation. 25 credits/mo covers a surprising number of transformations for a small SaaS.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare R2:
alternatives.text: R2 stores bytes; Cloudinary transforms them. If you just need a bucket, R2 is cheaper and simpler. If you need `?w=300&h=300&fit=crop` in a URL, Cloudinary does it out of the box while R2 requires you to build (or buy) an image resizing layer.

alternatives.name: UploadThing:
alternatives.text: UploadThing handles the upload flow; Cloudinary handles post-upload processing. For a media-rich app you might use both — UploadThing for the upload UX and Cloudinary as the CDN/transform layer — but if you must pick one, Cloudinary is the choice when transforms are a core feature.

entries.name: Tigris

fields.Limits: ~5 GB storage · egress caps on free · check current

prose: S3-compatible object storage with edge caching — pairs cleanly with Fly.
entries.pick: your compute runs on Fly.io and you want object storage that automatically replicates to the regions where your app instances run — no CDN configuration, no cache invalidation logic. Globally distributed by default with an S3-compatible API, so migration from R2 or AWS S3 is a find-and-replace on the endpoint.

alternatives.name: Cloudflare R2:
alternatives.text: Both are S3-compatible with free tiers, but Tigris is built for multi-region replication out of the box while R2 serves from a single location (fronted by Cloudflare's CDN). If you're on Fly, Tigris gives lower latency without extra config. If you're on Cloudflare Workers, R2's native bindings win.

alternatives.name: Backblaze B2:
alternatives.text: Tigris is hot storage with edge caching; B2 is cold archive. Tigris costs more per GB but delivers faster reads globally. Use B2 for data you rarely access; use Tigris for assets your users fetch on every page load.

entries.name: Inngest
prose: Durable functions, retries, cron — no Redis babysitting.
entries.pick: your app needs durable background functions with automatic retries, cron scheduling, or fan-out — and you refuse to manage Redis or a separate queue. Ship `inngest.createFunction()` alongside your Next.js/Remix app and get step-level observability for free (~50k steps/mo).

alternatives.name: Trigger.dev
alternatives.text: Inngest is higher-level: you declare steps and it handles retries/replay; Trigger.dev gives you a full serverless runtime for long-running jobs with more control over execution. Pick Inngest when you want zero-infra orchestration; pick Trigger.dev when your jobs run minutes-long or need custom Docker images.

entries.name: Trigger.dev
prose: Long-running Node jobs with observability.
entries.pick: your background jobs are compute-heavy or long-running (AI inference, video processing, multi-step pipelines) and you want a proper serverless runtime with the v3 SDK's built-in observability, log streaming, and retries — without managing workers or VMs.

alternatives.name: Inngest
alternatives.text: Trigger.dev gives you a full execution environment (think "serverless Sidekiq") so jobs can run for minutes/hours; Inngest caps individual steps and is better for short, event-driven orchestrations. Choose Trigger.dev when job duration or custom dependencies matter more than declarative step graphs.

entries.name: Upstash QStash
prose: HTTP queue that wakes serverless endpoints.
entries.pick: you just need a reliable HTTP message queue to wake serverless endpoints on a schedule or after an event — no SDK lock-in, no runtime to deploy. QStash is the lightest option here: POST a message, it delivers with retries and delay. Ideal for Vercel/Cloudflare apps that can't hold open connections (500 msg/day free).

alternatives.name: Inngest
alternatives.text: QStash is a dumb pipe (deliver this HTTP request later with retries); Inngest is a smart orchestrator (run this multi-step function). Pick QStash when your logic already lives in an endpoint and you just need guaranteed delivery; pick Inngest when you need step-level state, fan-out, or cron built in.

entries.name: Pipedream / n8n Cloud
prose: Glue APIs together without writing glue code.
entries.pick: you want to glue third-party APIs together (Stripe → Slack, GitHub → Notion) without writing integration code. Pipedream's low-code builder lets you wire triggers and actions visually, with a generous free tier that covers hobby/startup volumes.

alternatives.name: n8n Cloud
alternatives.text: Pipedream is fully managed and has deeper pre-built API integrations; n8n Cloud gives you a self-hostable escape hatch and more complex branching logic. Pick Pipedream for quick, managed API glue; pick n8n when you want open-source ownership or heavier workflow logic.

entries.name: n8n (self-host)

fields.Limits: Fair-code OSS self-host · cloud has free trial then paid

prose: Workflow automation + agent graphs without Pipedream caps.
entries.pick: you want Zapier-level workflow automation you fully own — run it in Docker on your homelab or VPS with zero per-execution fees. Best for complex multi-branch automations, agent-style graphs, or when Pipedream's free tier caps become a bottleneck.

alternatives.name: Pipedream
alternatives.text: n8n is open-source and self-hostable so you pay only for compute; Pipedream is managed but locks you into their execution limits. Pick n8n when you need unlimited executions, data sovereignty, or want to extend nodes with custom code without vendor limits.

matrixCells.limits: Fair-code OSS self-host · cloud has free trial then paid

entries.name: Sentry
prose: Error tracking with source maps. Boosted via Pack.
entries.pick: your app ships JS/TS bundles and you need stack traces that point to *your* source lines, not minified garbage. The 5k errors/mo free tier covers side projects; the GitHub Student Pack bumps you to ~50k + Team features for serious staging environments.

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.text: PostHog shows what users *did*; Sentry shows what *broke*. Install both — they complement, not compete.

alternatives.name: Better Stack
alternatives.text: Better Stack alerts you the endpoint is down; Sentry tells you the exact unhandled promise rejection on line 42 that caused it.

entries.name: Axiom
prose: Structured logs that don't melt your laptop.
entries.pick: you want to `console.log` structured JSON from your backend and actually *query* it later without running Elasticsearch or paying Datadog prices. ~500 GB/mo free ingest is absurd — you won't hit it on a solo SaaS. Axiom's query language (APL) feels like KQL and returns in seconds.

alternatives.name: New Relic
alternatives.text: New Relic is a full APM with traces/metrics/dashboards; Axiom is a focused log-query engine that's faster to set up and won't nickel-and-dime on seats.
